newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo tried to rein in rogue trader - manager.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo tried to rein in rogue trader - manager.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp tried five years ago to rein in former chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, but the losses from his unauthorised deals continued to grow to a record $2.6 billion, a Sumitomo manager said at Hamanaka's trial on Monday.

Hamanaka, once feared and admired as the most powerful man in the world copper market, pleaded guilty last month to fraud and forgery in deals that Sumitomo said were part of a complex, decade-long series of unauthorised trades.
Hamanaka's lawyers have argued that lax controls at Sumitomo were also partly to blame for the massive losses.

Testifying at the second session in Hamanaka's trial on Monday, Yoshio Takeuchi of Sumitomo's credit control department, said as long ago as February 7, 1992, Sumitomo set a limit of 100,000 tonnes, or about 300 billion yen ($2.46 billion), on the volume of copper warrants Hamanaka and his team could hold on the London Metal Exchange.
Takeuchi said Hamanaka repeatedly asked his superiors to raise or remove the limit, adopted after overseas traders alleged Sumitomo was trying to manipulate prices, but his requests were denied.
"Sumitomo was trying to straighten up its image towards the industry by setting the limit," he said.
He said Sumitomo officials also asked Hamanaka if he was manipulating the copper market and he denied the charge.
Speculation continued to surface, however, that Hamanaka was using his warehouse stocks and shrewd derivatives deals to keep world copper prices artificially high.
The limits also failed to halt Hamanaka's off-the-books deals, which he finally confessed to his superiors in June 1996 as U.S. and British investigators began to close in on him.
When Sumitomo fired him a few weeks later, it estimated his unauthorised positions were in the red by $1.8 billion.

His disappearance from the market sparked a frenzy of speculative copper selling, however, and London prices plunged to their lowest levels in two-and-a-half years. This further cut the value of copper Hamanaka had bought.
By September, when Sumitomo had finally closed out nearly all of Hamanaka's positions, the loss had ballooned to $2.6 billion.
In Monday's court hearing, Hamanaka lawyer Yutaka Miyake suggested that, if Sumitomo had not been in such a hurry to close out Hamanaka's positions, its losses may have been lower.
He noted that world copper prices started rallying again just a few months after Sumitomo said in September that it had disposed of Hamanaka's positions.
Takeuchi countered, however, that the market would not have rallied until it was clear Hamanaka's positions had been sold.
"If we had liquidated the positions more slowly, other traders would have known what our positions were and they would have rushed to go short in the market," he said.

Takeuchi said Sumitomo set up a special team, working in cooperation with New York investment banking firm Goldman, Sachs and Co, to minimise the losses from Hamanaka's positions while completing their liquidation as quickly as possible.

Hidesato Sekine, the head of Hamanaka's legal team, said the defence also hopes to call witnesses to testify on the system of internal checks and controls at Sumitomo's Hong Kong office, which was involved in some of Hamanaka's unauthorised deals.

Hamanaka, appearing calm in a suit and tie, smiled politely at reporters as he left the courtroom but offered only a "no comment" in response to their questions. He has been free on bail since February 24.
